title: FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, causing temporary ground stop at airport
description: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has halted flights bound for Miami International Airport in Florida after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway
body: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has halted flights bound for Miami International Airport in Florida after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway on Wednesday evening.Departures heading to Miami were grounded just after 20:15 local time (01:15 GMT) and all but one runway at the airport was closed, according to the FAA advisory. Flights are expected to resume by around 22:00 local time, the FAA told the BBC.The airliner that ran past the runway arrived from Memphis. No injuries have been reported. The FAA is investigating the incident. The ground stop comes on the day before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year in the US.Flight delays in Miami reached one hour but appeared to be declining later Wednesday night. Passengers scheduled to travel on Wednesday night were encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport."We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," Miami-Dade Aviation Department spokesman Greg Chin said in a statement to the BBC.The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travelers in the country over this holiday week, according to the American Automobile Association. The Miami-Dade area is under a flood watch until late Wednesday night. Periods of heavy rain throughout the day are expected to cause flooding, according to the US National Weather Service.A nationwide ground stop earlier this month halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

schema.headline: FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, causing temporary ground stop at airport

title: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
description: Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health minist
body: Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.Footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the tanker had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.

schema.headline: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway

title: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle legal battle over French winery
description: Image source, ReutersByNardine SaadBrad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vine
body: Image source, ReutersByNardine SaadBrad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vineyard, which unfolded amid a bitter divorce."We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," said the Hollywood stars' representatives in a joint statement.They bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.In the lawsuit, Pitt, 62, argued that Jolie, 51, acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to a Russian oligarch. She counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.The settlement announced on Wednesday resolves both of their respective legal actions."Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," said the statement from their representatives.Pitt's lawsuit had accused Jolie of seeking "to inflict harm" on him when she sold her stake in their co-owned vineyard, which he claimed had forced him to partner with "a stranger with poisonous associations and intentions".The Fight Club star said he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes in the venue without the permission of the other.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Jolie and Pitt wed at Château Miraval in 2014It was alleged that Jolie had sold her share to a Luxembourg-based spirits manufacturer controlled by Russian oligarch Yuri Shefler, without Pitt's knowledge.Jolie hit back with her own lawsuit, accusing Pitt of grabbing her by the head and attacking two of their children during a 2016 private jet flight trip.Pitt also verbally abused and poured alcohol on his family during the flight from France to Los Angeles, her lawsuit had alleged.Her lawyers alleged Pitt began shouting, accusing her of being "too deferential" to their six children - aged eight to 15 at the time.Pitt was not charged following a police investigation into the incident and he denied the allegations.They reached a divorce settlement late last year after an eight-year legal battle.It is understood that Pitt's litigation with Stoli Group, a beverage company owned by the Russian oligarch, is ongoing.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Zahara Marley Jolie and Angelina Jolie at a film festival At the time of their 2014 marriage, Pitt and Jolie were among the most lucrative names in Hollywood.They met on the set of the 2005 film Mr and Mrs Smith and were soon dubbed Brangelina by the press.The marriage was Pitt's second after a relationship with Friends star Jennifer Aniston. It was Jolie's third, after actors Billy Bob Thornton and Jonny Lee Miller.Jolie adopted her first child, Maddox, from Cambodia in 2002 a few months after he was born. Pitt later adopted him after he and Jolie had begun their relationship.In 2005, the pair adopted daughter Zahara from Ethiopia when she was a few months old.The couple's first biological child, Shiloh, was born in Namibia in 2006.Their son Pax was adopted at the age of three from Vietnam in 2007, and twins Knox and Vivienne were born in 2008.Since the couple split, four of the six children have legally changed their last name to Jolie rather than Jolie-Pitt, according to court filings citied by Hollywood press.

schema.headline: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle legal battle over French winery

title: Trump’s accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show
description: Image source, ReutersByThomas Copeland and Alison BenjaminBBC VerifyDonald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidi
body: Image source, ReutersByThomas Copeland and Alison BenjaminBBC VerifyDonald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows.Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible.The period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement.The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold".Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation.But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO.Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk".Nvidia's share price surged 31% on Monday following Huang's return. About $1tn (£763bn) was added to Nvidia's market value, but the company's shares are still trading below their value before reports of Huang's alleged affairs began to circulate.However, concerns remain among both Republican and Democratic politicians about Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US controls over the export of advanced computer chips to China, as well as Trump's involvement in getting him reappointed as CEO.Image source, Getty ImagesNvidia's chip technology and investments have been critical to the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, leading to it becoming one of the world's most valuable companies.The firm now represents more than 6% of the S&P 500 share index, according to State Street financial services. This makes it the second most valuable company on the index after Apple, whose shares Trump's accounts also frequently trade.Nvidia also ranks highly in many global indices, meaning that investment accounts held around the world, including pensions, are likely to include its shares.Our analysis of Trump's Nvidia trades does not include other investment products held by him which may include its shares.Trump made at least $2.2bn (£1.7bn) from a variety of investments and commercial activities, according to the financial disclosure report for the first year of Trump's second term.Barbara Perry, a presidential historian at the University of Virginia's Miller Center, told the BBC there is "no precedent for this," adding: "It's beyond anything we've ever seen in the presidency."Additional reporting Becky Dale

schema.headline: Trump’s accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show

title: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiersByOlga Ivshina and Yaroslava KiryukhinaBBC Russ
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiersByOlga Ivshina and Yaroslava KiryukhinaBBC RussianAt least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years.Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army  were accounted for in the Rosstat files.Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.How we came to a figure near half a millionThe Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesIn most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed.Additional reporting by Ilya Barabanov

schema.headline: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war

title: Hera mission images from asteroid crash show stadium-sized crater
description: The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.The extensive damage was cause
body: The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.The extensive damage was caused when a Nasa spacecraft hit the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022. The asteroid posed no threat, but this was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision."The crater is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular," said Dr Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist, who is on the Hera science team."It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to actually finally see what happened. And as a crater person, I can also say it's beautiful."The original 2022 crash test was carried out by a Nasa spacecraft called Dart which hurtled into Dimorphos at 14,000mph (22,000km/h).It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 6,200 miles long (10,000km), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.Dimorphos is about 150m (500ft) wide and was partly chosen as the target because it is one of an asteroid pair -  it orbits around a larger space rock called Didymos, which is about 730m (2,400ft) wide.The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.Before the collision, it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.A key objective of the Hera mission is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, in order to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth."It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team."We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."Hera's arrival on the scene is helping scientists answer many more questions too.Not only did the collision alter the shape of Dimorphos, it also changed the way it moves."Before the Dart impact, Dimorphos was more like our own Moon - so it was always showing the same face to Didymos, and it was behaving quite nicely," explained Raducan."Now it's very, very chaotic - it's tumbling. Imagine a barrel that you throw down the stairs, and the barrel is rolling and it's moving, and basically that's what Dimorphos does right now around Didymos."Hera has also taken detailed images of Didymos, revealing its surface in detail."The gravity at the surface of Didymos is about 40,000 times less than the gravity on Earth," said Naomi Murdoch, who is on the Hera mission team."We can already see some fascinating and complex geology. We can see regions of boulders."The smallest details that we can make out in these images are about 3m in size. So that means that all the boulders that you can see with your eyes are at least 3m big, and some as big as 10m. So what we're seeing here is boulders the size of cars and buses sitting on a world with almost no gravity."Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.The biggest, which measures more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city."We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who has worked on both the Dart and Hera missions."The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth."The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added."But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that."Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids - a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long.Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface.This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

schema.headline: Hera mission images from asteroid crash show stadium-sized crater

title: Protesters call on Israel to free Palestinian student held without charge
description: Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Mahdi Tunsi appears by videolink in front of his attorney Nasser Odeh during his hearing at the J
body: Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Mahdi Tunsi appears by videolink in front of his attorney Nasser Odeh during his hearing at the Jerusalem District Court on TuesdayByKaty WatsonReporting fromEast JerusalemIsraeli students, activists and academics are calling for the release of a Palestinian undergraduate who was taken from his university dormitory by Israeli police earlier this month and has since been held without charge.Mahdi Tunsi, a 26-year-old sociology and criminology student at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, appeared in an Israeli court in the city on Tuesday - a hearing that was held behind closed doors.Israeli police say he was arrested "concerning ties to an act of terrorism".Authorities have requested what is known as "administrative detention", which allows the Israeli state to detain people indefinitely without charge on the basis of secret evidence that they cannot see."We definitely think this is a political arrest," said Dr Yael Berda, one of Tunsi's university professors.Tunsi, a Palestinian resident of occupied East Jerusalem who works with well-known Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups, was arrested a month after Israel held an election that saw Arab-led parties win a record 19 seats in parliament, the Knesset, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition lose its majority.Since then, Berda said she had seen an intensifying campaign against Palestinian rights.Image caption, Knesset Member Dr Ofer Cassif was one of the those gathered outside the courtOutside the Jerusalem District Court on Tuesday, demonstrators waved placards with a black-and-white image of Tunsi, while crying out "shame" in unison."There's no due process - [administrative detention is] a sugar-coated term for being kidnapped and held as a hostage," said Dr Ofer Cassif, a Member of the Knesset representing the Arab-led Joint List alliance."We must all stand firm against such crimes. It's unacceptable."Since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, which triggered the Gaza war, the number of people in administrative detention has more than doubled.In October, there were more than 3,100 in administrative detention, according to Israel Prison Service figures published by Israeli rights group HaMoked. Most of them are Palestinians from the occupied West Bank.Israel says that its use of the policy is compliant with international law and a necessary preventative measure to combat terrorism.Image caption, Protesters held signs calling for Tunsi to be freed in Arabic and HebrewIn a statement, Israeli police said they would "not elaborate further regarding the investigation" into Tunsi.He appeared via video link from prison - his hair and beard shaved off. His friends also said that he was without medication as well as his glasses, despite a judge requesting them to be brought to him in detention.The Israel Prison Service said it acted in accordance with the court's rulings."When the process was complete and all the necessary approvals had been received, the detainee's lawyer was told he could pass the eyeglasses to the detainee immediately, subject to security procedures," it added.Berda asked to enter the courtroom on Tuesday but was denied entry. According to Berda, not even Tunsi has been told of the evidence against him.The judge has said more time is needed to consider the state's request for administrative detention. A decision is expected in the coming days.Image caption, The judge has said more time is needed to consider the state's request for administrative detention"If they have evidence, have them bring it or release him," said Berda."That's why we're demanding his immediate release or moving it to a criminal track where he could defend himself."Berda said that while Tunsi could not vote in Israel's general election because he is not an Israeli citizen, he was "engaged" and very supportive of Arab parties' involvement."Mahdi is one of the best human beings I know," said Noga Kaplan, who studies with him at the Hebrew University."He has a really pure heart and is very passionate about his studies."Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Protesters demand the release of Mahdi Tunsi outside the Jerusalem Central Court during his hearing.After Tunsi's arrest, the Hebrew University issued a statement saying it was notified a few minutes before it took place."The university is not a party to the legal proceedings involving the student, and we do not have information that would allow us to comment on the circumstances leading to the arrest or on the ongoing legal proceedings," it said.It added that it was concerned for Tunsi's well-being and hoped "that the matter will be resolved promptly and that his rights will be fully respected throughout the process".Tunsi is a resident of Silwan, a neighbourhood in East Jerusalem where, in recent years, Palestinians have been evicted by Israeli authorities, who say their properties were built illegally. Israeli settlers have since moved into some of those properties."Political organisation stopped after October 7 because people were getting super scared about the consequences," explained Kaplan."Mahdi saw studying as one of the ways to speak about it in class.""He didn't do a lot of public stuff because what's happening now is his biggest fear."

schema.headline: Protesters call on Israel to free Palestinian student held without charge

title: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 76 held hostage for 17 hours
description: De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly". He flew into the northern city to
body: De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly". He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation personally. He could be seen flanked by the commanders of the operation with a handgun strapped to his belt, in footage released following its conclusion.De la Espriella said the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in but had refused. Earlier in the day, the assailants had freed 10 of the hostages, among them elderly women. But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces teams prepared to enter the building, located in a popular shopping centre. Local media report that, as well as asking for safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (£1.5m) and armoured vehicles.De la Espriella said they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their plan to rob a cash-laden armoured car had been foiled. "It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.Johan Correa, one of the rescued hostages, described to local media how the gunmen, who he said had been disguised, had entered the supermarket, where he worked."We had just started our shift when some guys dressed as police officers came in and started robbing the place," he said. "They were robbers, but we thought they were police."He added that he and other hostages had been locked in a cold storage room, face down with their hands tied. "We were there for more than four hours, lying on the floor with our hands tied, and it was a really tough experience."Another employee, Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo, told Caracol radio that the assailants wore masks and had been armed with guns and knives.Velázquez said the gunmen repeatedly threatened the hostages, telling them that they had rigged the exits with explosives. He said that "thank God" they had been rescued, describing moments of tension as they heard explosions and a helicopter flying above.  Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building as people kneel with their hands behind their heads.It is unclear from the photos whether those kneeling are hostages or the hostage-takers. Local media report that the authorities feared that some of the gunmen may have tried to pass themselves off as hostages as the rescue mission unfolded. The identities of the four arrested have not yet been released.The hostages are being reunited with their families after being checked over by medical teams, according to the mayor of Cartagena.Many anxious relatives had spent hours waiting for news outside the perimeter place around the supermarket by security forces. A woman called Sandra told Caracol that her 76-year-old mother was one of those being held hostage. Sandra's mother - among a group of elderly people released after six hours - was reunited with her daughters and grandchildren.Footage recorded by local media showed bystanders cheering as some of those freed were escorted to ambulances waiting nearby.But with around 20 people still inside the building, tension outside rose and police said they had to stop some of the relatives from breaching the perimeter.

schema.headline: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 76 held hostage for 17 hours

title: The US pastor who wants to see women's right to vote overturned
description: "Patriarchy is in accordance with the way God made the world." That is the view of Pastor Doug Wilson, a conservative minister who the US Secretary of
body: "Patriarchy is in accordance with the way God made the world." That is the view of Pastor Doug Wilson, a conservative minister who the US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth calls his mentor.Speaking to the BBC from his base in Moscow, Idaho, Wilson explained his view that a society led by men is "a very great blessing". It's a perspective Christians who disagree with him say is based on a fundamentalist understanding of the Bible, which promotes the subjugation of women.A self-described Christian nationalist, Wilson believes the US should be a theocracy, with gay sex criminalised, abortion outlawed, and people of other faiths unable to hold public office.In the past he has delivered a sermon on "The Lost Virtue of Sexism," arguing that the Bible says women should be excluded from leadership of the church, and certain roles in civic affairs. And as part of his views on the division between the sexes, he would like the 19th Amendment of the US constitution, which granted women the right to vote, to be repealed, something his detractors say is anti-democratic.The vast majority of Christians support women's right to vote, and dismiss his message as misogynistic and extreme.Rev. Canon Dana Colley Corsello, the vicar at the Washington National Cathedral, rejects Wilson's understanding of what the Bible says about women's roles."In my mind, there is no biblical precedent or standing for what [Wilson has] proposed," she told the BBC."I'm married, I have a husband, I have children. My husband and I are complete equals in everything we do."Have the American Pope and the American administration fallen out?Pete Hegseth brings combative style as face of Trump's war in IranBut while Wilson still represents a fringe perspective amongst Christians in the US, some of his views have been gaining support.The denomination he co-founded, the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches (CREC), has around 150 churches in the US. It's a drop in the ocean compared to the 350,000 or so other Christian congregations the US. But Wilson says membership continues to rise.His influence has grown in part because of his connection to Pete Hegseth. The Secretary of Defence is a "proud member" of a CREC affiliated church, a Pentagon spokesperson told the BBC, adding that the "secretary very much appreciates many of Mr. Wilson's writings and teachings".Wilson says the two have "a warm relationship", although he stresses it is "largely a pastoral one, not a political one". Wilson has led prayer services at the Pentagon, including one in mid-November.Joining Wilson on stage, Pete Hegseth said "thank you for your leadership, for your mentorship, for the things you've started, the truth you've told, your willingness to be bold."Hegseth worships at the Washington, DC branch of Wilson's network of churches. And there are other members of the current administration that worship there too, according to Wilson.Of all his views, it is his statements on women's suffrage that have garnered the most headlines.Wilson favours "household voting", where the head of the home – usually a man – votes on behalf of their family.  It's the system used for elections within his church, although the women in Wilson's family do vote in civic elections in order to counter votes of liberals, he says.He says only in "odd" circumstances,  such as divorce or bereavement or "where the husband was a quadriplegic," should women assume the role of head of household. Just 7% of votes in Wilson's church polity are cast by women.When challenged by the BBC, he admitted it was a system that gave men "outsized influence".Wilson says that repealing the 19th Amendment is "low" on the list of priorities for him and his congregation. But, he adds, "we do think it".Julie Ingersoll, a professor of religious studies at the University of North Florida, says Wilson's beliefs are misogynistic and extreme - part of a world view that says women should be in complete submission to men in every part of their lives.It is extremely unlikely that the 19th Amendment would be repealed - it would require either a proposal from two-thirds of the House and Senate or two-thirds of the state legislatures. Three quarters of states would then need to ratify it.Still, says Ingersoll, the threat to women's rights should be taken seriously."It's not unlike the battle that they waged against Roe versus Wade," she says, referencing the Supreme Court decision that granted women the right to an abortion. It was overturned in 2022, after years of legal battles that restricted women's access to abortion."Thirty years ago, people would have said, oh, they're not gonna undo abortion rights."But they chipped away and they kept chipping away until they were able to overturn it. And I see this as directly parallel."While Wilson says overturning the 19th Amendment could take a century or more, there are conservative Christians who are pushing for women to have their right to vote removed more immediately.Last February, pastor Dale Partridge posted on Instagram saying "We will repeal the 19th Amendment within ten years".Partridge, who has around 900k followers across social media, credits Wilson as being someone who "broke the ice" for "strong politics and theology".Partridge has said that "the majority of women are not capable of responsible voting" because too many of them are liberal.He also frequently collaborates on podcasts with another conservative pastor named Joel Webbon.Webbon, whose New Christian Right YouTube channel  has more than 190k subscribers, has said that women's "desires are wicked". The solution, he claims, is to "take away women's vote". He was once friendly with Wilson, although they have since fallen out."Those guys have overshot by a long way," says Wilson of the two younger pastors. "They are disruptors and basically rage baiting."So what might be driving those who support the effort?Kelly Marino, an associate professor at Sacred Heart University who studies women's suffrage, says that the last decade has seen big wins for the women's rights movement, and "liberal political ideology" in general.But, she argues, "any time where there was sort of this peak of feminism, there've been people who respond aggressively and try to push back".Added to that are the high levels of uncertainty and conflict that have characterised the post-Covid period."I think there's been this craving for tradition and things that felt safe," Marino says.That, she says, can be seen in the popularity of notions such as being a "tradwife" or "soft girl", who reject career goals in favour of traditionally female roles of wife and mother.Marino says that while she doesn't think the constitution could be changed in the immediate future, the conversation around repealing the 19th Amendment is shaping the way people think about women's roles in general.Canon Corsello, the Vicar at Washington Cathedral, sees the midterm election results as a repudiation of the push against women's rights."Cultural issues did not translate in this election", she says. "When people are preaching love, empathy, inclusion... that actually resonated with people".Wilson's views have, however, been gaining ground beyond the US. The CREC has more than 30 churches internationally, including in Poland, Japan and Brazil.The latter country has seen its own movement of right-wing influencers pressing for the removal of women's suffrage, with some leaning on religious language to make their point.Wilson wants to continue expanding his brand of Christianity around the world, and has recently accepted a church in England into his network.While CREC churches in each country have their own distinct characteristics, Wilson says their core beliefs are the same.When it comes to the US, he says his ideal scenario would be for his congregations to "to practice what we believe in the church and for outsiders to look at that and envy it and say, man, that seems like a good system".

schema.headline: The US pastor who wants to see women's right to vote overturned

title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
description: Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early tra
body: Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down by closing time. The tech-dominated Nasdaq closed 0.6% lower.The declines came amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment, which has rattled investors in recent weeks.Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and Microsoft closed the day lower, though Meta and SpaceX were in positive territory by the end of the trading day.Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased. At close, it ended up 3.4% lower.The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia's CEO after revelations of his extramarital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs. But share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry. Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres.Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off."It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending, but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management.Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.Shares in Anthropic continued to trade below the $83 they debuted at last week, while Amazon shares fell by just over 3%.The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday.

schema.headline: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify

title: As foreign troops withdraw from Somalia, could al-Shabab take over?
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Some analysts fear Somali security forces may not be able to handle the nation's security without ext
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Some analysts fear Somali security forces may not be able to handle the nation's security without external supportByBasillioh RukangaSomalia is facing a fresh test of its stability as foreign troops begin withdrawing, funding for its security forces comes under pressure and a bitter political dispute threatens to derail plans for the country's first direct democratic elections in decades.The combination of challenges has raised questions about whether the government can defend itself against Islamist militant group al-Shabab while managing growing divisions among political factions.Some analysts fear the situation could embolden al-Shabab, which is affiliated with al-Qaeda, and potentially allow it to seize control of the capital, Mogadishu.The group already controls large parts of the country despite the presence of about 12,000 African Union (AU) troops supporting the government.The withdrawal of foreign forces, alongside the activities of clan-based militias aligned with rival political factions, has heightened concerns about the government's ability to maintain control.Ugandan troops, who make up the largest contingent of the AU force, began withdrawing last month, with the country expected to complete its withdrawal by next year.Ethiopia, another major contributor to the AU mission with over 7,000 troops, is also reportedly planning to withdraw about 3,000 troops. The US, which had earlier announced cuts to funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has since said it is extending it for a year. Washington contributes about a quarter of $500m UNSOS's annual budget, which supports Somali security forces, AU missions and individual troop-contributing nations.With military support uncertain and the government facing mounting political challenges, analysts question whether Somalia's security forces are ready to stand on their own.The concerns were heightened recently when al-Shabab claimed to have killed hundreds of elite Somali soldiers in an attack. The government acknowledged the attack but did not disclose the number of casualties.Abdisalam Guleid, a former deputy director of Somalia's National Security Agency, told the BBC the security situation was increasingly precarious.He warned that the withdrawal of foreign troops could leave Mogadishu vulnerable to a takeover similar to that of Afghanistan by the Taliban in 2021, following the withdrawal of US and Nato forces."I don't think Mogadishu will be able to defend itself. The Taliban style [takeover]… that's the most likely scenario I can envision now," he said.The Taliban took over control of Afghanistan between 6-15 August 2021 in a rapid offensive, following the withdrawal of US and NATO forces.Such a scenario has played out in Somalia in the past, Guleid explains.Somalia has experienced the collapse of central authority before.In the early 1990s, clan-based rebel groups advanced on Mogadishu from several fronts, forcing then-President Mohamed Siad Barre from power.His overthrow triggered a devastating civil war and a prolonged humanitarian crisis. The collapse of state institutions subsequently created conditions in which Islamist militant groups, including al-Shabab, were able to expand their influence.Guleid says Ugandan troops have been central to preventing a similar collapse since their first deployment to Somalia in 2007.They played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns, while protecting strategic installations, including the airport, seaport, government institutions and diplomatic missions.Troops from Burundi, Djibouti, Kenya, Sierra Leone and Ethiopia later joined the AU mission, while countries including Turkey and the US maintained separate military deployments and provided training and equipment to Somali forces.But Guleid argues that years of international assistance have not translated into sufficient military independence for the Somali government.He says the authorities have become so reliant on foreign protection that they have neglected to adequately prepare their own forces to take over.Somalia's Information Minister Abdifatah Qasim Mohamud rejected suggestions that the country would be unable to cope with the withdrawals.He told the BBC that Somali troops had already taken over some positions vacated by Ugandan forces and were prepared to assume greater responsibility for the country's security.He says Somalia could not depend indefinitely on foreign troops for its protection."I believe there is no reason for concern over this issue. There will be no change in the country's security situation or in the areas they have vacated," he said.President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has also been seeking continued international backing.During a visit to Uganda on 23 November, he and President Yoweri Museveni called on the international community to continue supporting Somalia to consolidate security gains.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Uganda troops were first deployed to Somalia in 2007Not everyone believes the withdrawal will necessarily result in a security collapse.Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa argues that years of international military support have helped Somalia establish the institutions needed to take greater responsibility for its security.He says the withdrawal will provide an opportunity to assess how much progress has been made.It will also force Somalia's political leaders to put aside their differences and take greater responsibility for the country's future, he adds.But other analysts warn that the timing could hardly be worse.Omar Mahmood, an analyst at the International Crisis Group, says Somali forces are  under considerable pressure as they fight al-Shabab while attempting to take over positions previously held by foreign troops.This is a major undertaking for an army that is still developing, he says.The military is also facing pressure in the Bay region of the South-West state, where forces loyal to ousted regional President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed have been fighting the federal government.The withdrawal of Ugandan troops from the Lower Shabelle region could create further security challenges, Mahmood adds.Mahmood further points to the long-delayed elections, which need to be secured, as another issue compounding the security situation.Somalia has been attempting to move away from an indirect electoral system in which clan elders select lawmakers, who then elect the president, towards a system of direct voting.Beyond the military situation, Mahmood says, the government must also resolve a growing political dispute over the timing and format of the country's elections.But the proposed changes have divided the government and opposition, with disagreements over how the elections should be conducted.The dispute escalated this year after the president pushed through constitutional amendments extending the presidential term from four to five years, effectively delaying the next elections until 2027.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Al-Shabab militants still pose a big threat against the governmentThis month, the Supreme Court ruled against the extension, ordering political leaders to agree on an electoral roadmap within 30 days and to hold elections within three months.Somalia says it rejects the decision.A day before the ruling, the president dismissed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed. They have since challenged the dismissals at the East African regional court in Tanzania.Mahmood says the political and security crises are closely connected, with the absence of consensus over the elections making it harder for the government to focus on the fight against al-Shabab.Guleid also warns that the threat to Somalia's stability comes not only from the militant group but from clan-based militias increasingly challenging the federal government."Today, we have clan loyalists fighting alongside al-Shabab against the federal government," he says.He added the country's leadership appears unable to anticipate the scale of the challenges ahead.Who will fill the gap left by foreign partners?Somalia's security challenges are compounded by its heavy dependence on international financial support.Latest data from its finance ministry shows that donor grants amounting to $878.8m accounts for two-thirds of its planned $1.36bn budget in 2026.Despite that, the ministry said it had only received about $314m of grants in the first nine months of the year, equivalent to 35% the expected annual aid. Mahmood believes that although some international military support is declining, other partners could help bridge the gap through bilateral agreements and continued assistance.But Guleid is sceptical that countries such as Turkey, Qatar and Egypt could quickly replace the military and financial contributions of Uganda and the US.He argues that Somalia's dependence on external support makes it particularly vulnerable when international partners change their priorities.That dependence has also contributed to increasingly strained relations with some foreign governments.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Somalia's challenges are compounded by its heavy reliance on foreign supportSomalia accuses the United Arab Emirates of funding armed groups and undermining its sovereignty, in the latest dispute involving an external power with significant security and economic interests in the country.The UAE has rejected the criticism and hit back at the Somali leader, describing him as an "outgoing president" in reference to the dispute over his presidential mandate.The two countries formally severed ties earlier this year, although the UAE has long been an important security and economic partner in Somalia.For Egesa, the withdrawal of foreign troops could ultimately provide an opportunity for Somalia to demonstrate how much progress it has made in rebuilding its security institutions.He believes the staggered departure of troops will allow Somali forces to assume responsibility gradually, while also forcing rival political factions to work together.But Guleid remains far less optimistic.He argues that unless Somalia addresses its military weaknesses, political divisions and growing influence of armed groups, it risks losing the security gains made.For now, it faces the difficult task of fighting an entrenched insurgency, managing rival political interests and preparing for a contentious electoral process, all while some of military partners are preparing to leave.Whether Somalia can withstand these pressures without renewed instability remains an open question.You may also be interested in:

title: Israeli strike kills senior Hamas security official and family in Gaza City
description: Wednesday's strike in Shati caused extensive damage to the Abu al-Ouf family's apartment.Photos showed the exterior wall and several interior walls we
body: Wednesday's strike in Shati caused extensive damage to the Abu al-Ouf family's apartment.Photos showed the exterior wall and several interior walls were destroyed, with rubble and broken furniture left scattered across the floor.An interior ministry statement said that Abu al-Ouf was killed along with his wife Noura, 41, and their daughters Yusra, 15, and Jana, 13.It condemned the attack as a "heinous crime" and accused Israel of targeting security personnel in Gaza "in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society".Hamas's internal security service is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting the group's infrastructure and rooting out informants.Israel's military said in a statement that Abu al-Ouf was a "significant figure" who had served as "a key source of expertise" in efforts to restrict Israeli counter-terrorism operations in Gaza."His elimination is a blow to the apparatus's leadership capabilities and follows yesterday's elimination of his commander," it added.On Tuesday, an Israeli drone strike in western Gaza City killed Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service.He had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid in Gaza City by Israeli special forces.Near daily Israeli strikes continue in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed in October last year.At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

schema.headline: Israeli strike kills senior Hamas security official and family in Gaza City

title: California warns of flooding as King Tides peak over Thanksgiving
description: Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday. Water levels across
body: Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday. Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding.Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US. Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area.In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding.Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data.King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day.While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record.Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said. On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding. Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said. "Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added. The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina.The US department store chain Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened. The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people. The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia. Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada said.King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too.

schema.headline: California warns of flooding as King Tides peak over Thanksgiving

title: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
description: North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close, in a row over
body: North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close, in a row over sanctions.It followed Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp in the eastern city of Wonsan, which is attended by Russian and Chinese children among other nationalities.The camp has been accused of involvement in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.North Korea's state-run news agency KCNA called the sanctions "a blatant hostile act".Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.Confirming the expulsion, KCNA said: "The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours."The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997. It was closed during the pandemic and remained shut for six years.

schema.headline: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row

title: US Army says controlled lead azide explosives blast in Iowa was 'huge success'
description: President Donald Trump said shortly after the blast that reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations". "The Army's controlled, mitiga
body: President Donald Trump said shortly after the blast that reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations". "The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media.Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa, ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising. In a Wednesday evening update on X, the Army said that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) had issued the "all clear" around the plant and that there was no airborne lead detection following the detonation."Post-detonation surface sampling is underway, and results will be released once complete," the Army added. Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin also said on social media that in the hours after the detonation "all EPA air monitors continue to report a ZERO DETECT of airborne lead".The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation - this made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.No level of lead exposure is considered safe, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to harmful effects.Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC he felt "relieved" after the detonation.He watched the blast from his job at a manufacturing plant eight miles (12km) away from the blast - and monitored a camera at his two-bedroom home just one mile from the detonation site. "We did not feel anything. We did not see anything," Johnson said.Also eight miles away from Middletown, Sandy Mabeus closed the windows and the garage at her home, brought their outdoor cat inside and hunkered down. The family watched three separate live streams on iPads and televisions of the explosion as it happened."We did not feel or hear a thing here," she told the BBC, adding that she checked the videos to confirm it had actually happened."The waiting and wondering has not been a good thing for anybody in the area," she said. "Hopefully they had a very good result and we can just get on with things."Iowa farmer David Vandenberg lives about 20 miles from the blast site and said he first learned of the detonation around two weeks ago. The Army Corps of Engineers took samples from his yard and pond on Tuesday."I was listening this morning, and I did hear a rumble about nine o'clock," he told the BBC on Wednesday, but didn't see or smell anything.Vandenberg expects officials to return to take more samples but "was happy to see that the blast was relatively contained. "I think the effects will be minimal"Illinois Governor JB Pritzker said on X that his state was "seeing little to no impact" from the blast. In a press release, he said he was directing state agencies to remain on standby for any "unanticipated impact".The Iowa site is only 10 miles (16 km) from the Illinois border.But there is also caution from some. Iowa's incoming Governor-elect Rob Sand said there was "more testing to do" and called for "immediate transparency" to explain why the lead-up was "so chaotic and unclear".Sand said that any Iowans who have been impacted in any way "must be taken care of fully, right away".Cameron Hamilton, the Fema administrator, said there would be additional resources and testing in the coming days and weeks.In recent weeks, the US Army scheduled and rescheduled their detonation ahead of colder winter temperatures.It also warned locals of "potential exposure to toxic lead dust", which led to some panic. It instituted measures including an optional evacuation zone and a shelter-in-place advisory ahead of the detonation.The Army faced pushback from residents and politicians alike and there were legal challenges to prevent the detonation from going ahead on environmental and health grounds. But on Monday, the appeals court overturned a decision to halt the blast. It said that - while these concerns were valid - the risk from an unplanned explosion was greater.Sheila Flynn and Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu contributed to this report

schema.headline: US Army says controlled lead azide explosives blast in Iowa was 'huge success'
